subtopic: AMENDMENTS REMOVING LIMITATIONS RESPECTING DATE OF DEBT, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS REMOVING LIMITATIONS RESPECTING DATE OF DEBT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to restore the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to some measure of usefulness. Certain limitations in the original act regarding the date prior to which debt must be incurred in order to qualify have rendered it useless and inoperative. The amendments eliminate those limitations and restore the act as an instrument of some little usefulness which was intended in the original legislation.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: URANIUM
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT EXTENDING DATE OF PURCHASE TO 1966
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Will the minister make a statement on the announcement made in the United States this morning to the effect that the date of United States purchases of uranium has been extended to the year 1966?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: URANIUM
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT EXTENDING DATE OF PURCHASE TO 1966
speechtext:
In my previous announcements to the house regarding the uranium purchasing program I have made reference to the close relationship which exists with the United States atomic energy commission. One feature of this relationship has been the similarity between the uranium buying programs in Canada and the United States. The recent announcement of the United States atomic energy commission concerning the extension of its domestic uranium-buying program suggests that I should clarify the position with respect to the Canadian program.
It is not the intention of the government to extend the Canadian uranium-buying program at this time. In my announcement of last August concerning purchases under the special price contract arrangement I pointed out that there was a limit on the amount of uranium which the United States atomic energy commission would wish to purchase from Canadian sources. I made reference again to this limitation in my statement to the house on March 2 concerning modifications of the special price arrangement. The situation in this respect has not changed. The United States atomic energy commission has stated that the primary reason for the extension of its domestic buying program is the need to maintain ore reserves in the United States. For the most part, the mines found to date in the United States, while numerous, do not have large ore reserves. On the basis of current and projected production rates, the present reserves would be close to exhaustion by 1962 unless ore replacements are found. It is considered that
4326	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry this can best be accomplished by encouraging the continued search for new ore deposits. The Canadian position is quite different. Most of the new mines which have been discovered in Canada have very large ore reserves. Even when the current contracts are completed, these mines will have substantial ore reserves. The Canadian position differs in another respect, namely, the anticipated requirement of uranium for domestic use. Even on the basis of the most optimistic forecast that can now be made as to the role of nuclear power in the Canadian economy, our resources of uranium will be greatly in excess of our domestic requirements for many years to come and we shall need to obtain export markets. The anticipated level of requirements in the United States, both for military and civil purposes, is vastly in excess of the anticipated requirement in Canada.
With respect to the position of the Canadian producer after March 31, 1962-the present termination date for deliveries under existing contracts-it should be noted that the special price contracts contain a clause which provides that the purchaser will have an option to extend the contract. The house will appreciate the difficulty of estimating the level of uranium demand six years in advance of that demand. However, every effort will be made to clarify the position with respect to the exercise of these options at the earliest possible date. The government is anxious to ensure that this important new industry will have continuing markets beyond March 31, 1962.
Negotiations are now under way whereby the United Kingdom will obtain from Canada part of its requirements of uranium. This uranium will be supplied under an arrangement similar to that which now prevails with the United States atomic energy commission. The quantities involved will be supplied from the contracts which will be entered into under the existing special price arrangement. As the house is aware, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada have had a very close relationship in the atomic energy program since its inception. The proposed arrangement is a continuation of this policy of tripartite co-operation.
As regards the export of uranium to other countries, the house will recall that in my announcement of August 3 and my announcement to the house of March 2 I stated that the government would take under consideration the establishment of an export policy for uranium. I pointed out that because uranium can be used for military purposes it was considered desirable that an export policy should be established with due regard to security provisions. It is the hope of the


government that arrangements for the marketing of uranium for peaceful uses can be worked out within a suitable international framework. As the house is aware, a 12-nation conference was held in Washington during the month of March for the purpose of considering a draft statute for an international agency for atomic energy. Canada was an active participant in this conference. The statute agreed upon at that conference will be submitted to a general conference in September next, at which there will be in attendance representatives of all the member countries of the United Nations. In the circumstances, it is considered advisable that establishment of export policy should await the outcome of the discussions at the September conference.
My remarks up to this point refer to arrangements involving substantial quantities of uranium. The government is now prepared to consider arrangements for supplying research quantities of uranium to other countries under bilateral agreements.

Mr. Speaker, arising out of the question asked earlier as to whether Her Majesty the Queen

Inquiries of the Ministry might visit Canada, and in view of considerable conjecture in the press that Her Majesty may be contemplating a state visit to a foreign country in Europe, would the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs say what is the position under present constitutional practice? Does Her Majesty under those circumstances, as head of the commonwealth, consult with and receive the advice of her prime ministers or her ministers in other parts of the commonwealth, and their consent, before such a visit can take place?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROCEDURE FOLLOWED IN ARRANGING VISITS TO FOREIGN COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the practice has been for Her Majesty to have this government informed when she has accepted an invitation to make a state visit to a foreign country. That was done on the occasion of the visit to Norway last year, and we were informed as early as the end of last August that Her Majesty was accepting an invitation to make a state visit to Sweden this summer. It has never been the practice for the government of Canada to be consulted with respect to invitations that we presume were extended to Her Majesty through the channels of the United Kingdom government. We have been informed that the acceptance of these invitations had been made, but it has never been suggested that we should take the responsibility of advice to Her Majesty when she accepts an invitation as the sovereign of the United Kingdom. We have never felt that we should consult the governments of other countries when an invitation is being considered by His Excellency the Governor General as the representative of the head of the Canadian nation to visit a foreign country. In respect of those visits of Her Majesty it has not been the practice to regard them as visits being made on behalf of the commonwealth but rather as visits made by the sovereign of the state through the government of which the invitation was conveyed to Her Majesty.

A friend who heard last evening's debate asked me later if my quotation from Hatsell meant that the rules of the house were meant only for the protection of the opposition. The quotation from Hatsell which is included in Beauchesne's third edition at citation 818, though in the language of a century and a half ago, makes this point crystal clear. The government has two protections. It has its majority and it has the rules. The opposition has only the rules. That is the reason that we are obliged to place special emphasis on strict adherence to the rules. That is the reason for the tremendous weight of the responsibility that rests upon


the occupant of the chair in seeing to it that the one and only weapon available to the opposition is not lost to it. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am insisting on a strict interpretation of the wording of standing order *78 (1) which requires that clauses be taken up in their proper order.

I am ready to admit, Mr. Chairman, that there are occasions when I point out that May is an English authority and that there are many portions of May which are not applicable to the Canadian situation. However, Mr. Chairman, yesterday in one of the rulings that you made as chairman of the committee of the whole house, you relied on May. You relied on May not only in your statements to us during the argument on the point of order but you included your reliance on May in your report to Mr. Speaker. A proposal to postpone the only effective clause of a bill until the subordinate clauses have been considered, or to postpone part of a clause, is out of order.
I think the point is quite understandable to all that this clause 3 which sets up the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation is the operative clause. Without this clause there is no bill. Without this clause there is no point in discussing anything else. I therefore submit that to postpone consideration of that clause is-as May, your own authority, says-out of order. Mr. Chairman, I wish to give full support to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for the reasons he gave and for additional ones as well, because the point can be fully supported on the grounds that he put forward, and in my respectful submission it can be supported on additional grounds also.
We cannot get away from the provisions of rule 78. They have been referred to several times but we must begin with them on this point. Clause 1 reads:
In proceedings in committee of the whole house upon bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order; the preamble and title to be last considered.
It is only natural, Mr. Chairman, that you should look around for precedents, and no doubt you have in your mind what occurred here yesterday. I think I should begin with some observations on that subject. In the first place, I submit to you that there is no precedent open to you in this respect to justify the course that the government is seeking to follow here except what occurred yesterday. There are no earlier precedents. Indeed, the precedents are all to the contrary. If the government is to be supported in this present motion to postpone consideration of clause 3 of the bill, then precedents for it cannot be found outside of yesterday's proceedings in this house.
I draw your attention, sir, to the submissions you have already heard-I do not take the time of the committee to repeat them- that the provisions of rule 78 must be given very strict Interpretation. I simply recall to your mind what was said on that point yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition and what has already been said on the point by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
All that has been heard in debate on the bill so far in the committee has been a succession of three statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in each case moving a similar motion. I draw your attention to what was said in each case. I will do it as briefly as I can because I am now
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation coming to the question as to whether what is now being done is a consideration of a clause under the provisions of standing order 78. In that regard, I think you have a very good guide in what was said by the minister in each case. At page 4283 of yesterday's Hansard the minister said, in introducing the same motion in respect to clause 1:
Mr. Chairman, clause 1 is the short title clause, stating that the act may be cited as the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation Act. It is purely a formal clause and since we have had some six days of general discussion and a few days more of procedural discussion I move:
"That further consideration of this clause be postponed".
Mr. Chairman, the minister was not pretending that that was consideration. The whole pith and substance of that very brief statement was that consideration is not necessary because it is a purely formal clause. Now, in the face of that, surely, when the minister, as the speaker recognized, and the only speaker recognized by the chair on the clause, stands up and says that there is no consideration required of this because it is a formal clause, no one in this committee can then pretend, let alone seriously argue, that there has been consideration of the clause.
Then, let us move forward and recall what the minister said in introducing the same motion with respect to clause 2. It is to be found on page 4293 of Hansard, and reads as follows:

Mr. Chairman, clause 2 is the interpretation clause and is standard in form. It gives definition of the "board"; "corporation"; what a director means; what the minister means; the northern Ontario section; "Trans-Canada" as the abbreviation of "Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited"; and the definition of "western section".
I move:
"That further consideration of this clause be postponed.
What the minister was saying to you there, sir, was that there is no occasion for consideration of this clause because it is a purely standard clause, just a clause of definition, a standard clause that does not require consideration. Such was his submission. In the face of that, does anyone pretend, in the light of the course then taken by the government in moving the motion that the consideration of the clause be postponed, that there had been consideration? It is perfectly clear, sir, from what the minister said himself, he was arguing before you that consideration was not necessary.
Then, the last reference, Mr. Chairman, is to what the minister said in introducing the

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation motion which is now before you. At page 4311 of Hansard he said:
Mr. Chairman, section 3 establishes a crown corporation in the form usual for crown corporations appointed by the federal government. The president and the four directors are appointed. The head office of the corporation shall be in the city of Ottawa. The directors receive no salaries but are allowed their living expenses and the usual provisions are made for civil servants who may be employed entirely by the corporation.
Mr. Chairman, I move that further consideration of this clause be postponed.
Again, sir, the whole pith and substance of the minister's statement was that this was just the usual form of clause in reference to crown corporations. He contended no consideration is necessary; therefore he moved that consideration be postponed. Now, Mr. Chairman, in the face of those statements whose aim and purpose are crystal clear, it is not going to be pretended, I am sure, by any hon. member that consideration nas been given to the clause when the minister was saying throughout, in effect, consideration is not necessary; therefore, because it is not necessary he moved that consideration be postponed.
My submission to you is this, sir. The statement by the minister, which is all we have, is not consideration by the committee within the terms of standing order 78, clause 1. Indeed, it could not even be pretended that it is consideration by the minister, let alone by the committee of the whole.
Mr. Chairman, if you say that what occurred yesterday has established a precedent to dispose of that point I will take respectful issue with that view and say to you that what occurred yesterday, in my submission, is not a binding precedent; it is certainly not a contrary precedent. However, Mr. Chairman, if you do hold that there was a precedent created yesterday which precludes you from giving the interpretation to standing order 78, clause 1, in the light of the facts, that I am asking you to put upon that clause, then I move forward to the next submission.
I say to you, sir, that on a proper consideration of clause 3 of the bill now before us, that clause cannot be considered apart from the consideration of clauses 1 and 2 which the committee has now been precluded from considering by reason of the two motions of the government. We are being asked to say that further consideration of this clause be postponed. I submit to you that clause 3 has not been considered. I go farther and I say that clause 3 cannot be considered in accordance with any sensible interpretation of the word "considered" in the light of the action taken by the committee already in passing the government's motions to postpone consideration of clauses 1 and 2.
[Mr. Fleming.l
Now, Mr. Chairman, if you will look at the bill itself you will see that an understanding of clause 3 of the bill is impossible without reference to clauses 1 and 2. Clause 3 of the bill is a clause-perhaps it might be called the heart of the whole bill

by which there is created a crown corporation to be known as the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. The clause goes on to deal with the appointment of directors, their tenure of office and removal, the delegation of their powers to the president or general manager, the making of by-laws, location of the head office and directors' meetings, the payment of expenses, the appointment of a general manager, the employment of officers and servants and retirement from employment by the corporation.
Now, sir, I defy any member of this house to attempt consideration, within the meaning of the term as used in our standing order 78, of clause 3 apart from references to the two preceding clauses of the bill. When standing order 78 speaks about consideration it surely means sensible, intelligent, competent consideration. It does not mean wrenching a provision out of all context in the bill and trying to shut one's eyes to the meaning including essential definitions attached to terms in the section and other provisions of the bill. Therefore I say, sir, that the committee cannot, as matters now stand, give consideration to the provisions of clause 3 within the meaning of standing order 78 without reference to and consideration of clauses 1 and 2; and that is precluded.
I go further on my next point, sir, and say that the process grows as we proceed with the bill. We are at clause 3. The government wants to postpone consideration of clause 3 and to prevent any discussion of it whatever because you ruled yesterday that this motion is not debatable. Well, sir, we know what is going to happen. If consideration of clause
3	is postponed, then when we come to clause
4	the same thing is going to be attempted again by the government. I point out to you, and I think you must consider what has now become a settled course of action on the part of the government in the light of an unfolding pattern before our eyes of government purpose with respect to this bill in committee, that you have to look further and see what is going to be the effect of this motion upon the proceedings that are to follow.
This motion with respect to clause 3 of the bill would defeat any attempt at consideration of the subsequent clauses of the bill because, sir, this is the clause that sets up the corporation which was the original sole purpose of the legislation as indicated in the original

resolution placed on the order paper by the government some months ago.
Now, sir, look at the other clauses, clauses 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the bill. They could not possibly be considered apart from clause 3. If this motion is now adopted, I submit to you that this house is not in a position to give consideration to clauses 4, 5, 6 or 7 within the terms of standing order 78.
I do not intend to dwell on the point, sir, but just look at clause 4 for a moment. It refers to a corporation. That is the corporation in clause 3. In clause 4 it is referred to as a body corporate having capacity to contract and to sue and be sued in the name of the corporation. And then it proceeds to deal with the status of the corporation as an agent of Her Majesty to deal with the holding of the property by the corporation, and so on. Then we come to clause 5 of the bill which establishes the purposes and powers of the corporation. What corporation? The corporation created by clause 3 of the bill, and yet the committee is being asked to say that clause 3 shall not be considered.
Go further, sir, and come to clause 6 of the bill. Again you have a provision that the corporation may borrow money from Her Majesty and certain provisions are contained therein in reference to the making of any such loans. What corporation, sir? It is the corporation created under clause 3 of the bill, and we are being asked now to pass over that clause without any consideration. How can it be said then that consideration could possibly be given to clause 6 within the meaning of standing order 78 if this motion is now accepted by you?
Finally we come to clause 7 of the bill which provides-and I am hurrying over this, Mr. Chairman-that:
Pursuant to an agreement in that behalf made, with the approval of the governor in council, . . .
-between Her Majesty and Trans-Canada, the corporation may on behalf of Her Majesty make short-term loans to Trans-Canada. What corporation? It is the corporation created under clause 3 of the bill. How can it be pretended that the committee will be in a position to give consideration to clause 7 of the bill within the terms of standing order 78 in the light of the motion now proposed?
I submit to you, sir, that if you were to entertain this motion you would be in effect accepting a course of action by which the committee will preclude and disable itself from carrying out the duty laid upon it by standing order 78 with respect to clause 4, with respect to clause 5, with respect to clause 6 and with respect to clause 7. I submit that a motion so absurd on its face as that cannot
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation be in order. A motion that would in itself defeat the application of standing order 78 and preclude the committee from discharging the plain duty laid upon it by standing order 78 cannot be in order.
I will not dwell further, Mr. Chairman, on the point that this motion would achieve a highly ludicrous result. It goes further, sir. If you receive this motion it will defeat the rules and I think it is quite obvious, sir, that that is so intended by the government. The pattern has emerged. In reaching your conclusion on this point of order in the light of the submission to you made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and in the light of what I am trying to submit respectfully to you now, I urge upon you that you cannot close your eyes to what happened yesterday. You cannot close your eyes to the clear pattern of action revealed yesterday in the succession of motions introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The pattern is clear and you have to look at that course of action with respect to the other two clauses and with respect to its application to the succeeding clauses of the bill because we know that is the government's intention. The conclusion is inescapable that this course of action of the government prevents, and is intended to prevent consideration of anything in the bill. It would tear the rules; it would tear our parliamentary safeguards to shreds and tatters.
Now, sir, I said that you cannot close your eyes to clause 3 in reaching your conclusion as to whether you may accept this motion, and you cannot close your eyes to what happened yesterday or what it is the government's intention to do with respect to later clauses. Here I come to another point, sir. All this flows logically, indeed sir it flows inevitably, from your recognition of the minister on this clause.
I wish now, sir, to turn to two of the citations which were dealt with in part by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and to develop my own particular submission on them. The essence of our parliamentary institutions surely rests upon the maintenance of the rights of all in this house as defined by the rules. You have had an abundance of citations as to the essential part, indeed the vital role, played by the rules and their maintenance in their full integrity in the preservation of the essence of parliament. It is not just a matter of the dry bones of procedural questions. Here we are dealing with matters that go to the very heart and vitals of our parliamentary institutions.
Now, sir, let me turn to the famous citation No. 1 in the third edition of Beauchesne in which Bourinot is quoted as stating:

The question is not debatable and the Speaker is bound to accept the memorandum prepared by the Chairman of the committee. I shall read it again for the information of the house-[DOT]
And at that moment the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Arthur Meighen, rose to a point of order and said:
The statement was never submitted to the committee before being submitted to the chair. Surely it is not the rule of this house that whatever the Chairman says is the point of order is really the point of order under review either by the committee or the house. The point of order was as clear as day. The Chairman stated it before the committee clearly, and he puts it in a different way to Mr. Speaker. That was the first I knew of it. He should have put it to the committee.
Mr. Speaker Lemieux said:
I think I am bound to accept the statement of the Chairman.
Mr. Meighen replied:
Then appeals are useless.
Mr. Speaker Lemieux said:
The point of order is stated by the party who is to report it to the house, or when appeals are taken from the ruling of the chair, the Chairman states his point. The Chairman stated his point in this way:-
And then he goes on to read the report. Mr. Meighen intervened again. He said:
I speak with some diffidence, because it is some time since there was a precedent, but, I think it is the duty of the Speaker to decide a point of order.
Mr. Lapointe joined in the discussion and said:
Section 183 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms reads:
"In case of an appeal to the house, it is the duty of the Chairman-"
This is probably taken from the second edition which is the same as citation 428 of Beauchesne's third edition. Mr. Lapointe concluded:
I submit that even my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition should be amenable to the rules of the house.
Mr. Speaker Lemieux then said:
Might I respectfully call the attention of the right hon. gentleman to what May says under rule 14: "Note that the appeal from the Chairman's decision is to the house and not to the Speaker."
Then he put the question and the question was decided in the affirmative. I cite this just to point out to hon. members that whatever happens in committee of the whole, if it is an appeal from a ruling by the Chairman, that appeal is not to the Speaker but rather it is to the house. I resumed the chair merely for the purpose of taking the report and submitting it to the house which must

decide one way or the other itself, a right provided by the rules of the house.
As far as the question of disorder is concerned, it is provided by standing order 59, paragraph 4, that:
The chairman shall maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house; but disorder in a committee can only be censured by the house, on receiving a report thereof.
Now, it is to the latter part of this citation that the report apparently addresses itself. The report I have received is that "the chairman was addressing the committee when the hon. member for Eglinton rose on a question of privilege. The chairman stated that the question of privilege could not be raised while he was addressing the committee and directed the hon. member for Eglinton to resume his seat. This the hon. member refused to do."
To follow the procedure which obtains under our rules and practice with respect to a report of this kind, it is to allow the hon. member who is mentioned in the report to rise and explain. The hon. member for Eglinton was given that right. He stood up a moment ago and we heard him. Following that the practice is to the effect that the hon. member concerned in the report is to withdraw while the house decides what it is going to do about the report. Now, the hon. gentleman remained with us and I think we were all happy to see him with us. And the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), because he had been mentioned in the remarks made by the hon. member for Eglinton, explained further what the position was and so did the Minister of Finance. The Leader of the Opposition spoke too, but it was to indicate to me that what was before me was to decide whether or not the hon. member for Eglinton had a right to be heard on the question of privilege.
I think I have explained as fully as I can that it is not my duty at the moment to decide on that point. I have nothing to do with whatever has taken place in committee of the whole. All that I have to deal with is the report I have received and my duty consists merely of presenting that report to the house and this is what I have done. The matter is now entirely in the hands of the house and not in mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: And with respect to the rights of parliament to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Those rights of parliament, as I have said, may very well be interpreted only by the presiding officers, and when they make an interpretation it is, I think, a duty of parliament to uphold them until a later time when another incident may occur. In these circumstances there appears to be, as I understand it from a very brief reading of the precedents, a reference of the matter to a committee; there seems to be a case of the suspension of the hon. member, if the house so determines, for the remainder of the sitting or at whatever length the house might decide.
I presume, sir, that the former, that is the question of the reference to a committee, has to do with a reference more inclined to his own personal interest perhaps of matters such as have been raised on other occasions. If that is so, and if this house is to indicate its support of the presiding officers in their decisions, the only possible motion which can be made is one of suspension. It is with the greatest regret that I am obliged to make that motion. I therefore move:
That the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) be suspended from the service of the house for the remainder of this day's sitting.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Finance has moved a motion to the effect that the hon. member for Eglinton be suspended from the service of this house for the remainder of the present sitting. The hon. member for Kamloops rose and moved an amendment. I am informed that the motion to suspend the member is not debatable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I shall hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on the point of order, but before he speaks I would tell him that I have just been informed that it is not debatable by virtue of standing order 32.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point I shall confine myself solely to the question as to whether the motion of the Minister of Finance is debatable. If I establish my point with regard to its debatability I shall speak to the motion later, but I shall restrict myself at this time to the point of order as to whether or not this motion is debatable. I too, during the time we have had since this incident started to arise, have been reading the citations and standing orders that would seem to apply and I also sent to the library and got Hansard for July 31, 1944, when the former member for Parkdale was reported and suspended from the service of the house for the balance of that day. If Your Honour wishes the page, it is 5683 of Hansard for July 31, 1944.
Your Honour relies for your statement that the motion is not debatable on standing order 32. May I point out, however, that there does not seem to be any standing order that spells out the procedure in connection with the naming of a member. I realize that this is not what is technically called the naming of a member, but from standing order 34 (2) it is fairly clear that it is, with respect to something that happened in the committee of the whole, the same thing as would be applied in the house itself. Standing order 34 (2) reads:
Mr. Speaker or the chairman, after having called the attention of the house, or of the committee, to the conduct of a member who persists in irrelevance, or repetition, may direct him to discontinue his speech, and if then the member still continues to speak, Mr. Speaker shall name him, or, if in committee, the chairman shall report him to the house.


Then there is another standing order calling for a report by the chairman to the house of any alleged misconduct. The reason I read standing order 34 (2) is that, so far as I can find, that is the only place in our standing orders where the word "naming" appears. Now, if one looks at Beauchesne's third edition-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I say this, so that we understand each other? I do not think that in this instance the member concerned had to be named. He was not named. He disregarded the authority of the chair in committee, and whenever that is considered to be disorder and when there is disorder in committee according to standing order 59 (4), a report must be made. Since at that moment when I resumed the chair I merely had to read the report of the chairman to the house, I have no power to name anyone, but the house has it within its power to censure, in whatever form it sees fit, the member who is mentioned in the report of the chairman. As a result of that I take it that the Minister of Finance, as leader of the house, has moved the motion that is now before me. The hon. member will be good enough to address himself to the question whether or not this motion of suspension is debatable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are on common ground and in complete agreement that this is not naming because the incident took place in committee of the whole rather than in the house itself. But when we start to search the standing orders to find what course we will follow in a case such as this I think Your Honour will agree that we have to look at all of the standing orders that seem to apply. You are right in directing our attention to standing order 59(4) which says:
The chairman shall maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house; but disorder in a committee can only be censured by the house, on receiving a report thereof.
Now, whether it is naming, which this is not, or whether it is a case of the house dealing with the report that has come from the committee, the question arises, how does the house deal with it? There are citations in Beauchesne, limited in number, but nevertheless there are some that can give us guidance. The only standing order which seems to me to have application is standing order No. 30 which reads as follows:
If anything shall come in question touching the conduct of any member, or his election, or his right to hold his seat-

I make it quite clear that I am reading the whole standing order although those last two phrases do not apply.
-he may make a statement and shall withdraw during the time the matter is in debate.
I also draw your attention to citation 229 which is based on that standing order although, of course, it refers to it as standing order 36, which was the number of standing order 30 in the former rules. Citation 229 reads as follows:
Note that under standing order 36, the member shall withdraw during the time a matter touching his conduct is in debate.
I point out, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that both standing order 30, or 36 as it used to be, and citation 229 of Beauchesne, third edition, indicate that a matter of this kind is dealt with by a debate. Surely if it is dealt with in debate, or by debate, that involves a debate. Your Honour may say that you are stymied by standing order 32 because it does not include in the provisions from (a) to (1) thereof a reference to a motion of this kind. I do not think it is a matter of surprise that a motion of this kind is not included there because it does not come up very often. I do not think it has occurred since the occasion when Dr. Bruce was put out of the house on July 31, 1944. But please note that subparagraph (m) of paragraph 1 of standing order 32 says:
(m) such other motion, made upon routine proceedings,-
I am prepared to admit that Your Honour may try to rely on that phrase, that this is not being made on routine proceedings, but the question might be asked how have we got anything if we have not in effect reverted to routine proceedings?
-as may be required for the observance of the proprieties of the house, the maintenance of its authority, the appointment or conduct of its officers, the management of its business, the arrangements of its proceedings, the correctness of its records, the fixing of its sitting days or the times of its meeting or adjournment.
I am sure it is quite clear from what the Minister of Finance said that his motion was made in his view-I am not arguing its merits now-under the general provisions of the maintenance of the authority of the house. Because it comes in there, the maintenance of the authority of the house, and that, I emphasize, is under the section that spells out debatable motions, it seems to me it is clear that it is debatable. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to summarize, apart from the fact that the motion putting Dr. Bruce out was debated briefly on July 31, 1944, I would say that there are these three references: Standing order 30, which says that this is something that is dealt with in debate; citation
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation 229 of Beauchesne, third edition, which refers to the matter being in debate, and third, there is the provision in standing order 32 (1) (m) which says that motions dealing with the maintenance of the authority of the house are debatable.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I have some additional citations with respect to the debatability of the motion. I would refer you first to Beauchesne, third edition, citation 191, page 82. I had better read the full citation. It is as follows:
It is the practice in the House of Commons to bring up a question of privilege after prayers, and before the house has taken up the orders of the day. Only in very aggravated cases, requiring the immediate interposition of the house, will any business be suddenly interrupted. May says, page 241, twelfth edition, that "the proceedings of the house may be interrupted at any moment, save during the process of a division, by a motion based on a matter of privilege"-
Perhaps I might pause there to say that is exactly what was happening in committee.
-"when a matter has recently arisen which directly concerns the privileges of the house, and in that case the house will entertain the motion forthwith." Bourinot, page 303, quotes an ancient authority as saying: "Whether any question is or is not before the house, and even in the midst of another discussion, if a member should rise to complain of a breach of privileges of the house, they have always instantly heard him."
Then there is one further three line sentence in that citation which does not seem to have any bearing on this particular matter. If you turn to Bourinot, page 305, you will see the following authoritative statement:
The Canadian House of Commons, in its desire to deal promptly with all questions affecting its members, has generally waived the strict rules which govern matters of privilege, properly speaking, and given every possible facility for inquiry thereon.
May I pause there to say that it seems to me impossible to have an adequate inquiry without adequate discussion and debate. Continuing the citation:
When a member proposes to make a motion touching another member-
That is certainly what has happened in this case. The Minister of Finance has made a motion touching the member for Eglinton. -it is frequently found convenient that he should state his intentions in his place, and then give notice that he will move it when motions are called in due order on a subsequent day.
Again interrupting the reading, I may say that it is made clear elsewhere that the house may take it under consideration immediately and therefore it is not necessary to give notice. Therefore I make no criticism on that ground although I think it might be argued that it would be more appropriate to do so. However, we seem to be seized of this matter at once, but I point out that the

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation fact that you give notice would to my mind, at any rate, indicate that the purpose of giving notice is so that members can be adequately prepared to debate the matter. Now then, after the question of whether or not debate is allowed on such a matter, page 306 of Bourinot is absolutely in point, and it reads as follows:
When a debate on a question of privilege has been adjourned until a future day-
I would ask Your Honour to pay particular regard to this passage on page 306.
When a debate on a question of privilege has been adjourned until a future day, priority will still be given to it. This was done in the case of Louis Riel, mentioned in a previous page, and there are numerous precedents in the English and Canadian Journals illustrating the same point.
So that Bourinot is direct authority for the proposition that such a question is debatable because debate may be adjourned and, sir, if it is debatable then, of course, it is susceptible to amendment. It would, of course, be utterly improper, I think, in view of the importance of the matter and the desire to protect all matters touching upon the conduct and position of members, to dispose of such a question without a debate and without an opportunity to assert the contrary view which I have sought to do in the amendment that I have moved to the motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The two hon. members who have spoken on the point of order that has been raised have, I believe, confused a question of privilege which is raised as such by one complaining of a breach of privilege and concluding with a motion or by one making an attack against an hon. member and concluding by a motion which may be dealt with, because it is privilege, immediately or may be appointed for debate and disposal at another time, at which time an amendment may be moved or the matter may be referred to the committee on privileges and elections. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has quoted standing order 30 as having a bearing on the situation as it presents itself at the moment. Standing order 30 reads as follows:
30. If anything shall come in question touching the conduct of any member, or his election, or his right to hold his seat, he may make a statement and shall withdraw during the time the matter is in debate.
This is a standing order which is germane to the two standing orders, namely standing order 79 and standing order 80, which used to be under the one heading before the house sent the matter of controverted elections to the courts. They were under the title "Independence of Parliament". They affected the case where in a debate, while a debate is going on, an attack is made on a member. I think it

happened here in the last parliament and the next day the said member came to the house and made a speech and then withdrew. As a matter of fact I think it happened twice during the last parliament that standing order 30 was applied. But at this moment we are not in a debate and a member has not been attacked as to his conduct or his right to hold his seat or in anything pertaining to his election. What has happened is a question of disorder which arose in committee. It is the matter of disregarding the authority of the Chair. That is the offence which has been reported by the chairman of committees. That report has been read to the house and the house has it within its power- because it may regulate its own proceedings and punish its own offenders-to decide what it will do. The hon. member for Eglinton had the right to explain, as in the case of Mr. Bruce who had been involved in a similar matter of misconduct. At page 5682 of Hansard of July 31, 1944 we find the following:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Bradette, chairman of the committee of the whole, reports that in committee of the whole Mr. Bruce, hon. member for Park-dale, during an address directed to the Prime Minister and the committee, stated that Bill No. 161, an act to provide for family allowances, introduced by the government, was a bribe to the people of Canada. Mr. Bruce was asked by the chairman to withdraw the word "bribe" which he had used. Mr. Bruce refused to withdraw that expression and appealed to the house from the chairman's ruling.
On a question of privilege, may I ask how the chairman made this report, when he was not in the chair at six o'clock? He was not even in the house.
I was in the house.
No; you just heard about it during the dinner recess.
On a question of privilege, I was in the house when the discussion took place and, more than that, I have read the report of Hansard.
I should have an opportunity to speak.

If a motion to censure a member were to be debatable and amendable, the purpose of the rule would be defeated. I am just told that in the case of Mr. Lacombe, the then member for Laval-Two Mountains, what happened was this. The hon. member concerned in the report has a right to explain and he has done so. If the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) had chosen, for instance, to say "Maybe I was too hasty" or if he had given the house to understand that if he had the thing to do over again he would not do it, the situation might be different. Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation could have moved that the statement made by the hon. member for Eglinton be accepted and the house would have been called upon, without debate, to vote on that motion immediately. Some one has to take the lead in these matters when the house has decided this point, and citation 136 of Beauchesne's third edition does indicate that the leader of the house has certain responsibilities with respect to this matter. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Because of the remarks that have just been made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that he appeals my ruling because it is scandalous that a decision of this kind be made without an opportunity of discussing the matter, may I say that these are difficult days for members on both sides of the house. I am going to volunteer certain remarks which I hope will help in the circumstances.
There are two sides in this house, members on my right and members on my left. No matter how serious, how difficult the political warfare or strategy between the two sides may be, I am now asking hon. members to keep in mind that the occupants of the chair are not concerned with and are not capable of intervening in the political warfare which takes place between the two sides. The occupants of the chair are forbidden by the rules from taking part in the debates. They have, for a long time, ruled themselves even out of debate in the committee of the whole. During the time they occupy the chair their constituencies are not to be heard through their voice. They are completely outside the discussion which takes place in the house.
Now, when a ruling is made hon. members have recourse to an appeal. No matter how useless they themselves may feel that recourse to be, nevertheless that is the only recourse they have. On the other hand, if they wish to criticize the occupants of the chair, not by way of appeal to the house on a ruling that has been made but because of

Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation their conduct, because of their partiality, because of their partisanship, because of any other reason, they also have a recourse and that recourse is, I think, one that should not be taken by devious means. I think it should be used in a straightforward manner. The occupants of the chair are deprived of so many rights as compared with other hon. members, for the purpose of doing their job, and if in the opinion of one hon. member or a group of hon. members the occupants of the chair are not deserving of the honour the house has given them; if they are not deserving of chairing any committees or the house itself; if they are not following the traditions and rules of the house as they should; if they are to be condemned in any way, I think the occupants of the chair are entitled to have their fate decided in the way the house has provided for centuries for doing this, and that is by way of a substantive motion after notice being placed on the order paper. I am sure it would be called at the earliest possible moment in order to have a debate brought about and the conduct of the occupant of the chair decided one way or the other.
1 would beg hon. members, notwithstanding whatever heat is developed in debate, to understand that is the position of the occupants of the chair. When the Leader of the Opposition says, "I want to appeal from your ruling", he has that right, and that right I grant him. But to add that he appeals my ruling because it is scandalous that a decision of this kind, that this motion is not debatable, be made without hon. members being able to speak to the matter, I think is going beyond his right in asking for an appeal, a right which I never refused to him.

that is on myself at the moment, I am very pleased to hear that and I want to thank him for that clarification.

I crave the indulgence of the house for a brief period on this bill. I should draw attention to the fact that 78 persons have been granted relief, or moved along one stage, in the last few minutes, but this is a case that was before parliament a year ago. On July 1 last year my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), discussed this case. Earlier in the session he referred to the fact that he had a letter from a Roman Catholic priest who had been a chaplain with the armed services, who had written to my colleague on behalf of this poor woman.
Apparently some hon. members on the other side of the house had some doubts about the accuracy of my colleague's statements, so in due course he received instructions from the priest to give whatever publicity he might wish to in connection with the case. I think hon. members at this point should pay attention to the letter which was put on Hansard on July 1 last year, as found on pages 5596 and 5597 of Hansard of 1955. The letter begins:
The poor lady has been notified that the Senate committee for divorces will hear her case on Friday, March 11. For the last three weeks, she had been on the verge of a nervous collapse.
Then further on:
The expectation was too much for her.
Then the hon. member made some interjections, and he was also interrupted.
February the 26th, she fell sick and the doctor had to be called. She was sent to hospital and since then has been in bed under treatment. She had a blood transfusion-
My colleague then remarked that they do not give blood transfusions for the fun of it. -daily serum and was seen by the hospital's psychiatrist.
Now, she will not be able to go to Ottawa this Friday. The lawyer asked for a written statement from her doctor and is going to present the committee with that letter. The doctor is even ready to go to Ottawa and testify if necessary.
What I am afraid of is that the adverse party tries to pull a fast one on her and win the case by default.
I simply think that it is criminal, even for a husband to frighten and torture his wife so much in order to get his goal that she totally collapses under the strain and tension. Such ignominious behaviour should be punished and I am really deeply shocked by the fact that our laws permit such events to happen.

I trust you to be able to stop a divorce that could be obtained under such circumstances. If you feel it may be useful to use my name and letters in that case, don't hesitate to do so.
May I thank you again for the care you took of that case.
I am very truly yours,
Capt. Rev. Robert M. Rivest, Headquarters Quebec Command, 3530 Atwater Avenue,
Montreal.
Following the discussion in the house by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) debate on the case was adjourned; then later the case came before the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills. I find that on the July 8 I had occasion to discuss the case in the house. Hon. members will probably recall that one of the investigators in this particular case was employed by a firm known as Reliable Detective Agency, and he and one of the other members of the firm were charged with fabricating evidence. I made some mention of that, and on page 5900 of Hansard of July 8, 1955, I find the following taken from the judgment of the appeal court:
The appellants, desiring to obtain evidence for the purpose of enabling a married woman to secure a divorce, planned to trap the husband into a false position from which adultery might be inferred or found if evidence was later given in some proceeding for divorce. This plan was to have a woman go to a room in an hotel, register under an assumed name and give the room the appearance of the bed having been occupied. She was not required to do anything more. The husband was to be lured by a pretext to the room and, when there, could be found by the two appellants, who would then be in a position to give evidence as to his being found there with the woman. In carrying out this plan, the appellants arranged with woman "A" to obtain the hotel room and perform her part of the plot, which she did. In the meantime, the appellants arranged with woman "B" to call the husband, under an assumed name, which was the name which woman "A" was to use at the hotel, and invite him to come to the room. This was done by woman "B", but the husband was suspicious. Woman "B" claimed to be a friend of the husband's sister, and the husband took the precaution of calling his sister as to the friend whose name he had been given over the telephone. Instead of going to the hotel room as invited the husband went to the police, with the result that the plan at that stage miscarried and it was the police who went to the hotel room, instead of the two appellants who were endeavouring to mislead someone.
The two men involved were Messrs. Pichette and Santerre.
Would the hon. member say what he is reading?

This is Hansard for July 8 of last year, page 5901. These are some details in connection with a case which was heard before Magistrate Strike in Ottawa. Hon. members will probably recall that the

case was appealed and Mr. Justice MacKay of the appeal court of Ontario ruled:
The first ground of appeal is that the crown failed to prove the intent necessary to constitute the crime charged. It is argued that it was necessary, under the charge as made, to prove an intent to mislead a court of justice, and that the intent proved in this case was not an intent to mislead a court of justice but, at most, an intent to mislead the divorce committee of the Senate, and parliament which might act upon a recommendation of the divorce committee.
Since that time, Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Senate has taken the necessary precautions so this will never happen again. At that particular time Mr. Justice MacKay apparently ruled that it was quite all right to fabricate evidence to mislead the Senate or mislead the House of Commons.
Is that what the judge held?
At that time, yes. The ruling was that the Senate committee was not a court of justice.
That is quite a different thing.

They were acquitted. The judgment of Magistrate Strike was reversed and the detectives were given a clear sheet. But it is significant, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Pichette, who was involved in fabricating evidence in the case I have mentioned, was one of the witnesses who came here a year ago to support the petitioner, but when the case was heard this year Mr. Pichette did not come. There were three detectives a year ago who accompanied the petitioner and, gave evidence on which the Senate committee reached a decision, but it is significant that although two of them came back this year, the one who was involved in the fabricating of evidence did not return.
This case was contested a year ago when it was Bill No. 184. We are a little behind this year because this year it is Bill No. 347 on the order paper. Mr. Pichette was examined last year and he was asked about the details in connection with the charge of fabrication of evidence. As found at page 28 of the proceedings of the Senate committee, counsel for the petitioner said:
I object to that, because there has been a judgment of the appeal court of Ontario and the charge of fabricating evidence has been dismissed: therefore, I don't think this question can be brought up today.
Then the chairman of the committee, Senator Ross, said:
It goes to the credibility of the witness.
Counsel for the petitioner replied:
But there was a judgment dismissing it.

So counsel for the defendant was not able to present his case as effectively as I am sure he would have presented it if he had been here this year. As I recall the situation, the wife has had a very difficult time in securing enough funds to defend herself adequately. On the other hand, the husband apparently has adequate funds available.
This is the first instance since I first came to parliament in 1940, Mr. Speaker, when, a lobby has been conducted in connection with a divorce case. I resent very much being lobbied by people without first being notified by them that they wish to lobby. I do not think those who are asked to judge a case of this sort should have one of the parties to a dispute walk into their offices without first telephoning or asking if it would be convenient to discuss the case.
I have had access to the evidence given before the Senate committee; and the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, of which I was a member at that time, reviewed the case. I think it is also significant, Mr. Speaker, that although a whole year has passed since the case was before parliament there has been no attempt to secure any new evidence. Hon. members might think it queer that the wife was not here to defend herself, but I think those who were on the committee last year realize what a terrific nervous strain it is for a woman who has been in poor health to be under the sort of attack that Father Rivest describes in his letter to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the miscellaneous private bills committee is taking a step at the moment for which I think it is to be commended, and I think this procedure should be made known to others who might be in a similar position.
There is another case before us in which $175 was ordered by the other place toward the expenses of the witnesses coming to Ottawa. They were here on a Friday, they had to come back on a Monday, and the amount of money was not sufficient to cover the actual out of pocket expenses; so the counsel in this other case has made two trips to Ottawa and has not had a five-cent piece. Our committee thought his request was only reasonable that he should have an opportunity to go to the appropriate court in the province of Quebec in order to see whether that court will not order the husband to make available to the wife sufficient funds to carry out her defence.
In connection with this case I submit that apparently the husband has adequate funds available to give both himself and his wife 
adequate counsel on the case. Since the evidence on which we have been asked to pass judgment here was collected quite some long time ago-it would appear as though it would be August 3, 1954; that will soon be two years ago-and since no new evidence has been produced in connection with this unfortunate case for nearly two years, I should like to have the co-operation of the house in supporting, as unanimously as we have these other 78 bills that have gone through, my motion which is seconded by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough):
That the motion be amended by leaving out the word "now" and adding the words "this day six months' hence" at the end thereof.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

As to the witnesses who gave evidence two years ago, were they the same witnesses with the exception of the one whose conviction was quashed in the court of appeal of Ontario, or were they a new set of witnesses to the same adultery?

Yes. Two of the three who were here on the previous occasion were back this year. The recommendation was granted on their evidence. The one witness who was involved in the case which went before Magistrate Strike was not back here, but the two who were here on the previous occasion were back, and the information which they secured nearly two years ago was accepted this year.

I realize that this may not be the time to go into this matter more than on the principle of this bill before us. I think it might be summarized by saying that with regard to the rights of the petitioner-and he has a right-this might not be the appropriate time to set it over, but it should again be considered by the committee responsible for considering these matters.
I might say that I, as chairman of the committee, have been highly pleased with the conduct of hon. members of that committee, having regard to the close attention they have given to matters of this kind. I might say that in cases where there are paid investigators the committee members give them added scrutiny, and I believe do a very good job.
I had hoped that the hon. member would allow this bill to go to the committee for consideration before moving his six months' hoist. As I say again, we must respect the petitioner's right. The petitioner has come before the Senate and the House of Commons. This time I notice that the case has come unopposed, that the respondent was called but did not appear.
No money available.

Nobody appeared for the respondent and the respondent herself did not appear. It has not come to my attention yet, as chairman of the committee, that any request was made for the $175, I believe it was, that was mentioned in another case by my hon. friend.
I think I am remembering the evidence correctly when I recall that this case was before the committee previously and in this previous instance I think it was the same army captain who was named as corespondent by the petitioner. The unusual part of it, the part that struck me at the time, was the fact that this lady worked in an establishment in which the army captain worked, as I recall it. This was a very warm
Private Bills-Divorce
summer night. Something I really could not get through my mind was why he should be going back there to her residence and giving as an excuse that he was going to have a bath-
Because he needed one.

It was a hot day. I could not understand why he should give that excuse as partial explanation for being in this lady's residence. I know at that time that really caused some concern and consternation amongst the members of the committee. Possibly they were influenced by that evidence in arriving at a decision.
I might say that, as I recall, the investigators appeared before the committee at that time and were very carefully cross-examined by the members of all parties. The evidence which they gave, in the opinion of most members of the committee, stood up very well. I do not think the co-respondent relieved himself of the duty which was imposed on him to explain why he was in the room of the wife of another man on this hot day, other than to take this bath.
I presume the evidence is very much the same. I also direct the attention of hon. members of this house to the fact that we must remember that the petitioner has petitioned to the Senate. The evidence was carefully gone into by the members of the Senate committee, who collectively or individually would be qualified to judge the validity of that evidence and come to a conclusion based upon the facts presented to them. In this particular instance the bill has reached the point of second reading in this house, and it would appear that the very active members of the private bills committee, such as the hon. member who has just spoken, would be able not only to do their duty but to show respect for the rights and privileges of other citizens in this country, in this particular case the petitioner, if the bill were permitted to go to the committee.
As I recall it, the petitioner is making his third petition, according to his right, to have this marriage dissolved. It is not a right that is particular to him but is a right extended to all citizens who live within the jurisdictions that require this procedure. I would ask that this bill be permitted, in the usual course of events, to go to the private bills committee for consideration. Possibly there my hon. friend might find something with which he could convince both the members of the committee and the members of this house that this bill should not be further considered. Let me conclude by saying that at this stage I really believe it would be well considered in the committee.

speechtext:
1.	Has any conference between top level authorities of the United States of America, the federal government of Canada and the province of British Columbia, been held to discuss downstream benefits in relation to power developments on international rivers?
2.	If not, are any conferences being arranged for?
3.	Has sufficient exploratory work been done to enable the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to report on the project for diversion of the flood waters from the Columbia into the Fraser river basin?
4.	If so, when will this report be available?
Answer by: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of
Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	No.
2.	The Prime Minister suggested to President Eisenhower during the conference at White Sulphur Springs, on March 27, that questions relating to rivers crossing the boundary be discussed by the two governments. I for one would not be satisfied even if Trans-Canada could build this pipe line with their own money, because I do not believe it is a wise thing to grant a monopoly to a private company to operate a public utility. But the situation is infinitely worse then that because the government is asking us to go to our taxpayers and ask them to contribute $9 apiece for every man, woman and child in order to help a private company to set up a private monopoly in this country, and they wonder why the opposition has reacted so violently to this measure which they brought into the house. What would our taxpayers say? For example, in my constituency there are approximately 50,000 people. What happened when we reached the resolution stage? Before any hon. member of the opposition had uttered one word or asked one question the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave notice that on the following day closure would be moved and the debate ended. Is that the way the opposition in this house should be treated? Indeed, is that the way the private members who support the government should be treated? The Ottawa Journal in an editorial published on May 29 comments on the effect of such statements in these words:
It is a grave thing for ministers to mislead the house; in Britain it is regarded as one of the deadly sins against parliament and public life.
Now, I endorse 100 per cent the opinion expressed in that editorial in the Journal. I believe it is a deadly sin against democracy and parliamentary life to mislead the members of this house by saying to them, "Let us not raise this question now. When we get into the committee stage you will have ample time to discuss every angle of this matter." And when we reached the committee stage, before anyone had uttered a word, the Minister of Trade and Commerce moved closure. That is one of the things that have stirred this country and given rise to a great many protests.
I come back now to what I consider to be the essential issue, and that is, what about the pipe line itself? We in this group stated in this house five years ago, and have stated over the years since then and from the beginning of this debate, that we want to see a gas pipe line built across Canada which is to serve the Canadian public. We have stated right from the beginning that we believe the only way in which that gas pipe line can serve the interests of the Canadian people
29, 1956	4455
Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation fairly and impartially, and the only way in which it can be retained in Canadian hands, is through public ownership. I made that statement, Mr. Chairman, on March 15 when the original resolution which was abandoned by this government was under discussion. I spoke these words:
So long as the issue of stock remains in public hands, there cannot be any guarantee that the ownership of the pipe line will remain in Canadian hands. We can ensure that this public utility can be retained in Canadian ownership only if it remains in public ownership.
Since that time, of course, that statement has been more than fully confirmed by what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said in this house and by what other hon. members have said. The only way in which we can assure the Canadian people that the gas pipe line will remain in Canadian hands, and therefore fully in Canadian control, is if it belongs to the people of Canada. There is no other way.
Now, that is one part of it and the other part of it is this. We talk about the reason for the gas pipe line. We want to serve the consumers across Canada. Our hon. friends to the left of us talk about the producers of gas in Alberta-
And the consumers.

-and the consumers also, of course. The question arises: If the Canadian people are going to be asked to raise approximately $130 million in order to finance this pipe line, then who should own it after it is built? That is an important question. That is the real issue. That is the bedrock question that has to be answered in this parliament and it is a question that cannot be answered by a snap decision. It is a question that requires full consideration without any closure because it is one of the most fateful decisions which this parliament will likely be called upon to make in this half century.
Think for a moment what has happened. We have had experiences in the past where Canadian resources have been sold down the river into private hands without much consideration and then perhaps half a century later people regretted that they had done so and could now do nothing about it. There are many examples of this sort of thing, if you look through the history of Canada, where people had reason to regret occasions when because of the illusory advantage of the moment they too hastily gave their resources away into private hands and then lived to regret it at their leisure.
What is the government asking parliament to do? They are asking us as public representatives to go to our taxpayers, the people

In the last few days a great deal has been said about some of the danger to the democratic procedure in this house and to parliament itself. So far as the opposition members are concerned, at times it may appear as if we have become overexcited on this issue. But let me say, Mr. Chairman, that if the hon. members who are now sitting on the other side and who are supporting the government found themselves sitting on this side of the house, as no doubt they will in due time, and if they were told that on an important issue such as this, which involves the expenditure of about $130 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money, they were not going to be able to take the time they required to discuss the issue properly, to inquire into all the details and to come to a sober and reasonable decision in the end, I am sure they would react with the same violence, perhaps greater, as has been witnessed in this house in the last few days.
Let me also say this. I address myself particularly to the private members on the other side of the house, for many of whom I have a great admiration. What has taken place in this house in the last few weeks has not been a credit to them because, even if they may feel obligated to support the measure that was brought into this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, they have no excuse whatever for allowing the government to ride rough-shod over the ordinary procedure of this house. Not only have they been a party to the attempt to break practically every rule in the rule book, but the abject obeisance with which they burned incense at the feet of the Minister of Trade and Commerce has come mighty close to breaking the first commandment.
This is confirmed by some of the statements that have been made in the heat of this debate by members of the Liberal party-when they are read in Hansard in more sober moments -by members of the Liberal party who, after all, have a great responsibility, because it is by the grace of the private member sitting on the Liberal side of the house that this government stays in power. Let there be no mistake about that. The government as a government has no status in this house. It is merely the temporary trustee of the public treasury. It is the members who support that government, or are willing to support it as long as they think the government is right, who give the government the power that it has.

No one in this country likes to see disputes between management and labour reach the point where such things as strikes and lockouts and all that go with them become involved. No one who has been through a strike, no one who has had some responsibility as an officer of a union in conducting a strike, has any illusions whatsoever about the unfortunate results of labour being forced to take that action. It is something that can be measured to a degree in the loss of pay cheques that ensues. It is something that can be measured by the loss of valuable industrial production. Measured by any one of those terms by which one can assess the effects and the implications of strikes and lockouts, it is an unfortunate and undesirable situation to have arise. It seems to me that no hon. member of this house who is interested in the welfare of the working people of Canada, in the growth of our country, in the increase of the real wealth which we as citizens may be able to enjoy in our proper share, should for a moment hesitate to endorse a measure which will in some degree at least remove the possibility of the advent of such things as strikes and lockouts.

That, Mr. Speaker, is the real argument in favour of the adoption of this type of legislation in Canada. By its adoption you have put the collective bargaining process in its proper role. You have taken out of the area of dispute the question of the right of the workers to organize and bargain collectively.
This legislation proposes to introduce into our federal labour law the principle which, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated when he introduced this bill, has been adopted in the legislatures of six of the ten provinces in this country up to the present time and which is in the process of coming into being in at least one of the other Canadian provinces.

When a principle has become as well established as this has through the long and bitter process of collective bargaining, why should this parliament hesitate any longer to put this into the form of legislation so that the process need no longer be continued for the minority of those who may not enjoy it as a right? As long as the parliament of Canada refuses to recognize that this sort of thing is a right of the workers of Canada, then just so long are we giving tacit recognition to the fact that employers who come within the field of federal labour legislation have the right to go out on union busting tactics and that in fact, as well as in law, the workers have not really the right of collective bargaining.
